trechos.texto: Close your eyes. Actually do it. For three seconds. What you're looking at is not nothing. There's a dark field sitting in front of you. Some drifting smudges, little sparks of blue and white if you press on your eyelids. That's still vision. Your eyes are shut, and the machinery behind them is running anyway, handing you a picture of the dark. Now try something harder. Try to see out of your elbow. Not feel with it, see with it. Work out what your elbow's view of the room looks like right now. You can't, and the reason isn't that your elbow's view is black. Your elbow has no view. There is nowhere in your head for that picture to go. That is the closest a person with sight ever gets to what someone born blind experiences. Almost everything you assume about blindness comes from the wrong image. You're picturing a room with the lights switched off and someone someone trapped inside it. But here's the thing, the person who has never seen was never given the room. Ask someone blind from birth what they see, and the answer comes back flat, and slightly impatient. There are no shapes, no shadows, no color. There's no darkness either. Because darkness is something you have to be able to see in order to sit in. Tommy Edison has been blind since birth. He spent years answering this exact question on camera, and keeps landing in the same place. There is nothing there, and he means that literally. Not as a poetic way of saying black. The proof shows up at night. When Tommy dreams, he doesn't see. He hears, he smells, he tastes, and he feels his way through the dream. Because his subconscious never learned how to see, and can't fake it. In 2014, researchers in Denmark collected dream reports every morning for four weeks from people born blind, people blinded later in life, and sighted volunteers. The people born blind reported almost no visual content, and far more sound, touch, taste, and smell than anyone else. They also reported significantly more nightmares. Now compare that to Christine Ha. She won Masterchef in 2012. She lost her sight in her 20s to an autoimmune condition called neuromyelitis optica, which took her optic nerves apart over about 7 years. She still dreams in full color, walking around independently the way she used to. In those dreams, she's still in her 20s because that's the last face she ever saw in a mirror. Waking up, she said, makes her sad, because for a few seconds it hadn't happened yet. Two people. both blind, and their nights are made of completely different material. Her brain kept the room. His was never issued one. But an empty room inside a brain doesn't stay empty. Vision is expensive. Close to a fifth of your cortex is tied up processing it, which makes your visual cortex the most valuable real estate you own. In a person born blind, that hardware doesn't switch off. It gets repurposed. In 1996, Norihiro Sadato and his colleagues published a study in Nature. They put blind braille readers in a PET scanner and watched their brains while their fingers moved across the dots. The primary visual cortex lit up. Not faintly. It behaved as though it were doing its old job. When sighted volunteers ran their fingers over the same raised patterns, their visual cortex did the opposite. It went quiet. It deactivated. For the blind readers, the part of the brain built to see was reading. Then it gets even stranger. Daniel Kish lost both eyes to cancer before he was 14 months old. He gets around by clicking his tongue and listening to the echoes off walls, door frames, parked cars. He rides a bicycle this way. In 2011, Laura Thaller, Stephen Arnott, and Melvin Goodale recorded the clicks and echoes of expert blind echolocators and played them back while scanning their brains. The calcarane cortex responded. That's the deep visual region, the first stop for signals arriving from the eye. their auditory cortex showed no equivalent response. The sound was being handled by the visual system. And then there's language. Also in 2011, Marina Bedny and colleagues at MIT found that in adults blind from birth, the left occipital lobe, right where vision is supposed to live, responded more strongly to real sentences than to scrambled speech. It was tracking grammar, behaving like a language area. So a brain that has never seen is not a brain with a hole in it. It's a brain that took the largest unused property it owned and rented it out to touch, to sound, and eventually to sentences. Before you file this under things that happen to other people, there's a complication inside your own head. Between 3 and 5% of people can't summon a mental image at all. It's called aphantasia. Ask them to picture an apple and they'll tell you everything about apples. There's just no apple. The interior picture you assume everybody has is not standard issue, and you have no real way of holding yours up against anyone else's. There's one question about all this that stayed open for 323 years. On the 7th of July, 1688, an Irish philosopher named William Molyneux wrote to John Locke. Molyneux's wife had gone blind, and he'd been turning something over. Suppose a man born blind learns to tell a cube from a sphere by touch. He can do it perfectly, every time, with his hands. Then one day, he's given sight. You put the cube and the sphere on a table in front of him, and you don't let him touch them. Can he tell which is which? Locke thought not. Molyneux thought not. And for three centuries, there was no way to find out. Then Pawan Sinha, a neuroscientist at MIT, set up Project Prakash, which finds children across India blind since birth from treatable cataracts, and operates on them. For the first time in history, Molyneux's man existed, and you could simply ask him. Sinha's team built 20 pairs of simple shapes out of toy blocks. Within 48 hours of surgery, a child would learn a shape by touch alone. Then, try to pick it out by eye. They couldn't do it. They performed at chance. The results went into Nature Neuroscience in 2011.

After 323 years, the answer was no. But there was a second half Locke never saw coming. Within days, sometimes within a week, the same children could do it easily. The bridge between what the hand knows and what the eye sees isn't installed at the factory. It gets built fast, but it has to be built at all. And it gets much harder to build the longer you leave it. In 1959, a 52-year-old Englishman named Sidney Bradford was given corneal grafts in both eyes. He had been blind since he was 10 months old. Two psychologists, Richard Gregory and Gene Wallace, wrote up what happened next. Some of it worked immediately, exactly as Project Prakash would predict decades later. Bradford read the time off the ward clock almost straight away because he'd spent his life reading a watch with his fingers. He sailed through a color vision test, pulling numbers out of a field of colored dots. Everything he'd already learned by hand came across in a day. Everything else refused to. Shown a drawing of a cube, he saw a flat pattern of lines. He asked the researchers what depth meant. They gave him a wooden brick and ran his fingers along it. And he understood the brick perfectly. then looked at the drawing again and said it wasn't the same thing at all. The optical illusions that fool every sighted person on the planet did nothing to him. Afterwards, he went quiet. He found the world drab and dirtier than people had let on. He kept identifying his tools with his eyes shut because it was faster. He died within two years of the surgery, after a long stretch of poor health. Mike May lost his sight at three, and got some of it back at 46. He's adapted about as well as anyone ever has. He still can't reliably tell a man's face from a woman's, and when someone walks away from him, he doesn't see them receding into the distance. he sees them shrinking, which puts the original question in a very different light. Tommy Edison has made the point better than any researcher. People spend enormous effort trying to imagine what his world is like and get nowhere. That, he says, is exactly how far he gets trying to imagine yours. The gap runs in both directions, and it's the same size in both directions. You're carrying a picture of the world built out of a substance you couldn't describe to him without running out of words. He's carrying one you'd have the same trouble receiving. So the real answer to what blind people see is not black. And it isn't nothing either. Because nothing is still a description of an empty space. It's that the question has nowhere to land. Close your eyes one more time, and that dark field comes back. Your brain handing you a picture of no light, which is still a picture. That's a thing you have. Then think about your elbow. That's the part nobody can show you.
